paper_a.title: Yet another proof of Brooks' theorem

paper_b.title: A short proof of Brooks' theorem

metadata.description: Both papers prove Brooks' theorem (every graph with chi=Delta+1>=4 contains K_{Delta+1}, equivalently: a graph with Delta(G)<=k and no K_{k+1} is k-colorable). Paper A (Rabern) uses a minimum counterexample with a maximal independent set M, extracting an induced K_Delta or odd cycle T from G-M and gluing two non-adjacent vertices in N(T). Paper B (Zajac) uses induction on |V(G)| together with a PathColor greedy procedure along a maximal path through non-adjacent neighbors of a vertex; it also adds an algorithmic version and a correspondence-coloring generalization absent from paper A. The shared theorem and the shared 'non-adjacent neighbors' trick make this a clean alternative-proof (AP) pair.

matches.explanation: Both nodes state Brooks' theorem. Paper A phrases the contrapositive ('chi(G)=Delta+1>=4 implies K_{Delta+1} subseteq G'), paper B phrases the standard form ('Delta(G)<=k, no K_{k+1} implies k-colorable'). These are the classical equivalent formulations of the same 1941 result; assumptions and conclusions translate directly under k=Delta. Note that paper A treats the theorem as the paper's own contribution to reprove, while paper B labels its TP419.1 origin as 'external' (Brooks 1941).

Both are proofs of Brooks' theorem but use different techniques. Paper A: minimum counterexample, maximal independent set M, induced K_Delta/odd-cycle T in G-M, glue two non-adjacent vertices in N(T) to get a smaller K_{Delta+1}-free graph H, color H by minimality, extend greedily to T. Paper B: induction on n, reduce to k-regular, pick non-adjacent neighbors x,y of a vertex v, build a maximal path P starting v_1=x,v_2=v,v_3=y, split into Case 1 (r=n) and Case 2 (r<n) and finish with PathColor. Both share the high-level idea of exploiting two non-adjacent neighbors that can receive a common color, but the global decomposition (M + T vs. maximal path + DFS-style cycle) is fundamentally different — exactly the AP pattern.

Composite L2 alignment under the matched proof parents. Setup parallels: PSP413.1 (minimal-counterexample + Delta-regularity from minimality) corresponds loosely to PSP419.1 (base case + reduce to k-regular by deleting a low-degree vertex and induction) — both reduce to the regular case. The 'non-adjacent neighbors' trick appears in both: PSP413.4 picks non-adjacent x,y in N(T) and forms H by adding xy if missing; PSP419.2 picks non-adjacent neighbors x,y of v (guaranteed because no K_{k+1}). After that the proofs diverge: paper A's PSP413.2/PSP413.3/PSP413.5 (extract T, rule out K_{Delta+1}-edge, color H and extend to T) have no analogue in paper B, and paper B's PSP419.3/PSP419.4/PSP419.5/PSP419.6 (case split on path length, PathColor along the path, cycle extraction in Case 2, bridge to G') have no analogue in paper A. The match is at the cluster level only — individual L2-to-L2 correspondences are mostly best-fits, not exact.

PathColor procedure — paper B's signature technical device for greedily coloring along a path while leaving the last vertex uncolored. Paper A uses ordinary greedy coloring on T and on G-D but never abstracts a path-color subroutine. This is a genuine paper-B-only contribution.

Brooks-type theorem for correspondence (DP-) coloring — paper B's Section-3 generalization to arbitrary list assignments and constraint graphs. Paper A makes no list-coloring or correspondence-coloring statement.

DFS-based linear-time Brooks coloring algorithm — paper B turns its inductive proof into an explicit O(m+n) algorithm (with Skulrattanakulchai-style data structures). Paper A is pure existence and produces no algorithmic counterpart.
